title: Does P ≠ NP imply both polynomial-space enumeration separations?
formal:
Is the following implication true for enumeration problems with polynomial-time checkable, polynomial-length solutions?
\[
\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\left(\mathrm{DelayP}\ne\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}}
\ \land\ 
\mathrm{IncP}\ne\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\right).
\]
Here DelayP permits polynomial delay and unrestricted working space, IncP permits incremental polynomial time and unrestricted working space, and the superscript poly requires the same enumerator to obey the timing guarantee while using only polynomial space in the input length. All classes use the deterministic RAM model defined below.
why: The question tests whether space can be an essential resource for efficient enumeration even when each solution is short and easy to verify. Fixing P ≠ NP asks whether this familiar decision-complexity separation already forces a time–space distinction for producing many answers.
status_note: The original conditional separation program remains open in the checked sources. This card now asks the precise implication from P ≠ NP, an announced editorial default after the optional hypothesis question received no reply. The July 2026 regularization theorem equates two classes already constrained to polynomial space, and the EXP/PSPACE construction drops efficient verification. Neither resolves the selected implication; later-work checks through 17 September 2026 were bounded.

importance.reason: A structural resource-separation question for two major enumeration classes, relating simultaneous output efficiency and memory bounds to P versus NP.

sentences: An enumeration problem has polynomial-length solutions whose validity can be checked in polynomial time.
Polynomial delay bounds each wait for the next answer, while incremental polynomial time bounds the cost of every initial segment.
The question asks whether P ≠ NP forces both timing classes to become strictly weaker when the same algorithm must also use input-polynomial space.
Output order is unrestricted, and the two separations may have different witness problems.
Known regularization and broader-framework results do not settle this precise implication, whose complete proof or refutation must be Lean-checked.

definitions:
A problem in \(\mathrm{EnumP}\) is a relation \(A(x,y)\) on finite binary strings whose membership is deterministically decidable in polynomial time and whose solution lengths satisfy \(|y|\leq p(|x|)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p\). On input \(x\), enumeration must output every element of the finite set \(A(x)=\{y:A(x,y)\}\) exactly once, produce nothing else, and terminate. No order is prescribed. Let \(n=|x|\) and \(N=|A(x)|\).

Use uniform deterministic random-access machines with a fixed finite program, integer registers, direct and indirect addressing, branching, comparison, addition, subtraction and multiplication. An arithmetic or comparison instruction on integers \(a,b\) costs \(1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+|b|+1)\rceil\); other basic instructions cost one. Input is explicitly encoded in finitely many initial registers, and all other registers initially contain zero. This fixes the source's bit-sensitive arithmetic and unit-cost random access conventions.

Space counts all bits of the registers through the largest accessed address, assigning at least one bit to each integer including zero. It also counts all retained output buffers and machine counters. Charging the stored input changes this by only a polynomial amount. A completed output is a finite bit string on an external write-only stream; the stream supplies no readable memory. Charge for writing its bits. There is no randomization, oracle or advice. The RAM model matters for unrestricted-space polynomial delay, where a growing dictionary can still support fast random access.

The class \(\mathrm{DelayP}\) consists of EnumP problems admitting an algorithm and a fixed polynomial \(q\) such that the time before the first output, between each consecutive pair of outputs and between the last output and termination is at most \(q(n)\). If there are no solutions, it terminates within \(q(n)\). The source stops immediately on its final output; charging polynomial terminal work gives the same class by retaining that final result until termination is established. Polynomial preprocessing is included in the initial bound.

The class \(\mathrm{IncP}\) consists of EnumP problems for which some algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) output the first \(k\) solutions within \(C(n+1)^b(k+1)^a\) time, for every input and every \(1\leq k\leq N\), and terminate within the same kind of bound with \(k=N\). Empty outputs require polynomial input time. The exponent may be any fixed integer and does not depend on the input. This is polynomial time in each output prefix, rather than a fixed polynomial delay independent of the number of earlier outputs.

A superscript \(\mathrm{poly}\) requires that the same enumeration algorithm satisfying the timing guarantee also use at most \(s(n)\) working bits at all times, for some fixed polynomial \(s\). In particular, its memory is independent of \(N\) and of the number of solutions already output. Without that superscript, neither class imposes a separate space bound. There are immediate inclusions \(\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\subseteq\mathrm{DelayP}\) and \(\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\subseteq\mathrm{IncP}\). The requested inequalities would make both inclusions strict, potentially with different witness relations.

For the background, \(\mathrm P\) denotes languages decidable in uniform deterministic polynomial time, \(\mathrm{NP}\) languages with polynomially verifiable polynomial-length witnesses, \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) languages decidable with polynomial working space and \(\mathrm{EXP}\) languages decidable in time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), all on ordinary Turing machines. The later regularization theorem concerns \(\mathrm{IncP}_1^{\mathrm{poly}}\), where the time for \(k\) outputs is bounded by \((k+1)q(n)\). It equates this class with \(\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\); it does not remove a pre-existing superpolynomial storage requirement.

The selected hypothesis is exactly \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Both separations must follow from this same hypothesis:
\[
\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\mathrm{DelayP}\setminus\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\ne\varnothing\bigr)
\ \land
\bigl(\mathrm{IncP}\setminus\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\ne\varnothing\bigr).
\]
The two witness relations may differ. Each relation and its algorithms are fixed before inputs; the polynomial space bound is in input length alone, not the number of outputs. The hypothesis cannot be replaced by a stronger conjecture about enumeration, by \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\), or by the desired separations themselves.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under P ≠ NP, a polynomially checkable and polynomially balanced relation for each separation, an enumerator with the unrestricted timing guarantee, and the impossibility of every enumerator simultaneously obeying that timing guarantee and input-polynomial space. A negative proof must establish P ≠ NP together with equality of at least one of the two class pairs. A separation only for uncheckable solution relations, a restriction on output order or access to a black-box generator, or the space cost of a particular algorithm does not satisfy the target.

context_blocks.text: Fast enumeration may accumulate a large history of answers, use it to generate new answers or buffer irregular output. The question asks whether this memory can be essential to the existence of a good timing guarantee. The memory consumption of one familiar algorithm is not evidence that every algorithm for its relation needs that much space.

Every EnumP relation can be enumerated in polynomial space by scanning all possible bounded-length witnesses and checking each. That procedure need not have polynomial delay or incremental polynomial time. The unknown issue is the simultaneous use of small space and the requested timing guarantee, not polynomial-space enumerability by itself.

If P = NP, prefix-existence tests for any EnumP relation become polynomial-time decidable. Depth-first search over candidate witness prefixes then enumerates solutions with polynomial delay and polynomial space. Thus all four classes collapse to EnumP under that hypothesis, and a separation would entail P different from NP. The converse implication is not supplied by the source.

Dropping polynomial-time solution verification changes the problem. The source can hide the answer to an exponential-time decision problem among exponentially many trivial outputs; a polynomial-space enumerator would reveal that answer in polynomial space. This gives a conditional separation under EXP different from PSPACE for the larger framework. Its special output cannot generally be checked in polynomial time, so it is not a witness for the EnumP-restricted target.

The July 2026 regularization theorem proves equality between polynomial-space linear incremental enumeration and polynomial-space polynomial-delay enumeration. Both sides already obey the same space restriction. It therefore does not prove equality, or strict inequality, between unrestricted-space and polynomial-space classes in this card.

Restricted black-box lower bounds measure algorithms that can access only a supplied generator, sometimes with an output-order constraint. The requested class separations permit arbitrary algorithms reading the relation’s original input and freely choosing the output order. The stronger restrictions in a black-box lower bound cannot silently be imported into this target.

The historical question allowed an unspecified complexity hypothesis. This card selects P ≠ NP and therefore asks a particular converse to the known collapse under P = NP. It does not claim that this chosen implication appears verbatim in the source.
